passages.original: Quibusita descriptis,nunc quemadmodum Marci , Tullii divisio Them istii partitioni conveniat explicemus.Locum igitur quem Cicero dixit a toto,a substantia Themistius esse proposuit.Uterque enim in diffinitione consistit,sive illa substantialia sit, sive descriptio.
passages.english: These things having been thus set out, let us now explain how the division of Marcus Tullius [Cicero] agrees with the partition of Themistius. The topic, then, which Cicero called "from the whole," Themistius proposed to be "from the substance." For each consists in definition, whether that definition be substantial or a description.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (e.g. "Them istii"). "substantialia" read as "substantialis".

passages.english: Indeed, the whole partition of topics by Marcus Tullius seems to be contained within the division of Themistius in the formula of the description above. Now the division of Themistius must be brought back to the division of Marcus Tullius. Much of it does indeed agree with Cicero's, as the earlier description also shows. But what remains of Themistius' division, if it [is referred] to
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the context suggests it continues "...to the order of the Tullian partition." "Themistui"/"Tbemistu" read as "Themistii".

passages.original: A forma Ciceronis, a parte, id est specie Themistii. A similitudine communis.A differentia Ciceronis, a toto vel a parte Themistii.A contrario Ciceronis,idem apud Themistium ab oppositis. Ab adjunctis Ciceronis, eumdem acommuniter accidentibus Themistius posuit. Ab antecedentibus et consequentibus, mixti cum pluribus. A repugnantibus Ciceronis, idem a Themistio ab oppositis dicitur. Ab efficientibus Ciceronis, a causis Themistii. Ab effectis Tu Ilii, a fine Themistii.
passages.english: Cicero's "from form" is Themistius' "from the part," that is, from the species. "From similarity" is common [to both]. Cicero's "from difference" is Themistius' "from the whole or from the part." Cicero's "from the contrary" is the same as "from opposites" in Themistius. Cicero's "from adjuncts" Themistius set down as "from common accidents." "From antecedents and consequents" are mixed with several [topics]. Cicero's "from incompatibles" is called by Themistius "from opposites." Cicero's "from efficient [causes]" is Themistius' "from causes." Tullius' "from effects" is Themistius' "from the end."

passages.original: Comparatio est, cum propter meliorem utilioremve,factum quod adversarius arguit commissum esse, dofenditur.Horum vero on:- nium sunt propriae differentia?, atque ideo minu- tissimæ divisiones quas rhetorum in his docendis explicandisque conscripti libri diligentius continent. Sed nos haec a M. Tullio sumpsisse sufficiat. Ad aliud enim tota operis festinat intentio. De quibus omnibus hoc inspiciendum est modo. M. enim Tullius causarum partes constitutiones esse demonstrat eo loco quo contra Hermagoram nititur, dicens, quod si generis caus;e partes non possunt recte putari, multo minus rectae [F.recte]partis causae partes putabuntur,Pars autem caus'P constitutio omnis est, partes causae constitutiones esse designans. Quare de re multa quaestio est, quomodo enim partes esse putabantur causæ. Si enim ita partes, ut species quomodo fieri potest ut in una causa plures constitutiones sint ?Nam species sibi invicem impermistae sunt.
passages.english: Comparison is when the deed which the opponent alleges was committed is defended on the ground of something better or more useful. Of all these there are proper differences, and therefore very minute divisions, which the books written by rhetoricians for teaching and explaining them contain more carefully. But let it suffice for us to have taken these from Marcus Tullius, for the whole aim of the work hastens toward something else. Concerning all of these the matter must be examined in this way. For Marcus Tullius shows that the constitutions [i.e. issues] are parts of cases, in that place where he argues against Hermagoras, saying that if they cannot rightly be thought parts of a genus of case, much less will they rightly be thought parts of a part of a case; "but every constitution is a part of a case," thereby indicating that constitutions are parts of cases. Hence there is much question about the matter: in what way were they thought to be parts of a case? For if they are parts in the sense of species, how can it happen that there are several constitutions in one case? For species are unmixed with one another.
passages.notes: "rectae [F. recte]": the edition's variant "recte" adopted. "constitutio" (Greek stasis) rendered "constitution", i.e. issue of a case. Several scanning errors corrected ("dofenditur", "on:- nium", "caus'P").
